newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq defies U.N., flies pilgrims to Saudi Arabia.
newsitem.headline: Iraq defies U.N., flies pilgrims to Saudi Arabia.

text.p: An Iraqi airliner carrying 104 Moslem pilgrims on Wednesday flew to Saudi Arabia in defiance of U.N. sanctions barring international flights by Iraqi aircraft.
Reporters saw a Soviet-built Ilyushin 76 take off from Rasheed airbase in the eastern outskirts of the Iraqi capital on its way to Jeddah airport in Saudi Arabia.
Jeddah airport officials had no immediate comment on the flight.
The pilgrims, all over 50-years-old, were defiant. Sheikh Ibrahim Dirbaz said he was determined to reach Mecca or die a martyr on the way.
Others said they were sick and could not stand the hardship of the 2000 km (1250 miles) land journey to Saudi Arabia. Of the 104 pilgrims, 40 were women.
Senior Iraqi officials, including two ministers, took part in a farewell ceremony before the pilgrims took off.

Endowment and Religious Affairs Minister Abdul-Muneim Ahmed Saleh said the sending of the plane to Saudi Arabia despite the U.N. trade sanctions was ..."a humanitarian endeavour and had no other purpose in mind ... There may be some problems but the aim is humanitarian.
"We call on our brethren in the Islamic world to take note of this unfair embargo which infidel countries have imposed and in which Arab and Islamic states are taking part," Saleh said.
The aircraft's captain Muayyad Younis al-Dibourni said he hoped ... "our Arab brethren (in Saudi Arabia) will welcome the plane."
U.N. sanctions were imposed on Iraq after its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Some 1,000 Iraqi Moslems left for Saudi Arabia by road on Monday for the haj, the first group from Iraq to perform the annual pilgrimage to Mecca since 1994.
Saleh said Iraq under quotas set by the Organisation of the Islamic Conference was allowed to send 20,000 pilgrims to Mecca per year... "but conditions of sanctions prevent us from doing so."
Pilgrim Abdulsahib Saeed, 63, said he was sick and needed to make the haj to fulfill one main pillar of his religion.
All Moslems should perform the haj at least once in their lives if they have the means. It is one of Islam's five essential obligations for believers.

The U.N. Security Council had rejected a request by Iraq to use its civil aircraft to fly this year's pilgrims to Mecca. It also turned down a plea by Baghdad to have part of its assets frozen abroad released for haj purposes.
Some two million Moslems perform the haj which reaches its climax next week.
The U.N. last week rapped Libya for a March 29 flight to Saudi Arabia in defiance of U.N. sanctions connected with the 1988 bombing of a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland.
This was the third year in a row that Libya violated the sdanctions by flying pilgrims to Jeddah.

The Libyan sanctions were imposed in 1992 because of Libya's failure to extradite two men charged in Britain and the United States with involvement in the mid-air bombing of Pan Am flight 103, which killed 270 people.
Diplomats in the kingdom say Saudi Arabia as custodian of Islam's two holiest shrines cannot be seen as denying any Moslem with a valid haj visa the right to perform pilgrimage.
